summary: Jesus is brought to the Roman governor under political charges. Pilate declares no basis for conviction, sends him to Herod, and receives him back mocked; political rivals become friends around the abused prisoner. Although Pilate repeatedly calls Jesus innocent, he capitulates to demands for crucifixion and releases Barabbas, imprisoned for revolt and murder. Simon of Cyrene carries the cross behind Jesus, while Jesus warns Jerusalem's mourning women of coming disaster. At the Skull, rulers, soldiers, and one criminal repeat the temptation to save himself. Jesus prays forgiveness, promises Paradise to the other criminal, and dies with Psalm 31's trust on his lips. Darkness, a torn temple veil, a centurion's declaration, mourning crowds, Joseph's burial, and the Galilean women's careful witness close the day before Sabbath rest.
whyItMatters: Luke presents crucifixion as public execution carried out by Roman authority through political cowardice, elite accusation, crowd pressure, and soldier violence—not as abstract tragedy or collective ethnic guilt. Jesus's kingship appears through mercy and trust rather than self-rescue. Even in catastrophe, condemned people, women, a conscripted passerby, a centurion, and a dissenting council member become morally visible.

context.author: The Gospel's anonymous author, traditionally Luke, narrating Jesus's Roman trial, crucifixion, death, and burial with distinctive innocence, mercy, and witness motifs
context.audience: Theophilus and a wider Greek-reading audience; the chapter confesses a crucified king within the Roman world and guards against collective blame
context.date: Commonly dated after Jerusalem's destruction in AD 70, around AD 80–90; dates in the 60s and into the early second century are also defended
context.setting: Pilate's Jerusalem proceedings, Herod's hearing, the route to execution, the place called the Skull, and a rock-cut tomb
context.literaryForm: Roman trial and execution narrative shaped by repeated verdicts, scriptural echoes, sayings from the cross, and burial testimony

outline.heading: Political charges before Pilate and mockery before Herod
outline.note: Accused before Pilate, Jesus answers 'So you say'; Pilate finds no basis and sends him to Herod, who mocks him after getting no answers

outline.heading: Repeated innocence verdicts, Barabbas, and Pilate's capitulation
outline.note: Pilate finds nothing worthy of death, but the crowd shouts 'Crucify! Crucify him!' and asks for Barabbas; Pilate hands Jesus over

outline.heading: Simon, mourning women, and warning for Jerusalem
outline.note: Simon of Cyrene is made to carry the cross; Jesus tells the mourning women to weep for themselves and their children, not for him

outline.heading: Crucifixion, forgiveness, mockery, and two criminals
outline.note: He says 'Father, forgive them' as he is crucified between two criminals; one insults him, the other asks 'remember me' and hears of Paradise

outline.heading: Darkness, torn veil, death, and witnesses
outline.note: Darkness and a torn temple veil; Jesus cries 'I commit my spirit' and breathes his last; the centurion calls him a righteous man

outline.heading: Joseph's tomb and the women's Sabbath preparation
outline.note: Joseph, a council member, asks Pilate for the body and lays it in a rock tomb; the women see it, then prepare spices

keyVerses.text: Jesus said, “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing.” Dividing his garments among them, they cast lots.
keyVerses.why: The prayer embodies Luke's mercy at the site of execution, while its important manuscript history calls for an honest note.

keyVerses.text: Jesus said to him, “Assuredly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise.”
keyVerses.why: Jesus answers a condemned man's future request with immediate personal hope.

keyVerses.text: Jesus, crying with a loud voice, said, “Father, into your hands I commit my spirit!” Having said this, he breathed his last.
keyVerses.why: Psalm 31 gives Luke's final word from Jesus the form of filial trust, not defeat or loss of control.

questions.question: Why do the accusations before Pilate sound different from the council's religious dispute?
questions.answer: Before the Roman governor, the accusers recast the case as national subversion, tax refusal, and rival kingship. Luke's Jesus did not forbid Caesar's tax in chapter 20, making that charge distorted. ‘Christ’ becomes ‘king’ because imperial law, not an internal theological disagreement, supplies the machinery of execution.

questions.question: Does Luke excuse Pilate because he declares Jesus innocent?
questions.answer: No. The threefold verdict exposes the injustice rather than absolving the judge. Pilate has authority, proposes punishment despite innocence, yields to pressure, releases a man imprisoned for revolt and murder, and hands Jesus over. Luke can stress innocence before Roman law while still depicting Roman capitulation and crucifixion as decisive responsibility.

questions.question: Who is responsible for Jesus's death—and who must not be blamed?
questions.answer: Luke names particular chief priests and rulers, an insistent crowd in this scene, Pilate's sentence, Herod's and soldiers' abuse, and Roman crucifixion. He also names Jewish dissenters such as Joseph, Jesus's Jewish followers, the women, and the people who mourn. Converting these specific actors into guilt assigned to all Jews across time is historically false, narratively contradicted, and antisemitic.

questions.question: What does Simon carrying the cross ‘after Jesus’ evoke?
questions.answer: Those leading Jesus away seize a passerby and lay the cross on him. Luke describes Simon bearing it opisthen—behind—Jesus, echoing Jesus's earlier call to take up the cross and follow him. Simon is not romanticized as seeking suffering; a forced task becomes an enacted image of discipleship inside a brutal event.

questions.question: Why does Jesus redirect the daughters of Jerusalem's grief?
questions.answer: He does not reject compassion. He warns that the city's coming siege will be so terrible that conventional blessings of fertility will invert, using Hosea's language of mountains covering people (Hosea 10:8). On one common reading, the green/dry tree proverb reasons that if this is done to the innocent Jesus, devastation around a guilty and combustible order will be worse.

questions.question: Why is ‘Father, forgive them’ footnoted or absent in some Bibles?
questions.answer: The saying is missing from some ancient witnesses and present in others; the evidence runs on more than one side. Its vocabulary and mercy fit Luke, yet omission and addition are both historically proposed. Modern editions often retain it in brackets or with a note; the manuscript question should not be hidden, and Luke-Acts teaches enemy forgiveness elsewhere regardless.

questions.question: What does ‘today you will be with me in Paradise’ mean?
questions.answer: Greek manuscripts originally lacked modern comma punctuation, so a minority reads ‘I tell you today, you will be…’ Most interpreters join ‘today’ to ‘will be’ because Luke repeatedly uses sēmeron for salvation arriving now, and the promise directly intensifies the criminal's future ‘when you come.’ Paradeisos, a word most think is of Persian origin, means a garden or park and pictures God's garden or blessed dwelling, not a full map of the afterlife.

questions.question: Why does Luke's centurion say ‘righteous’ when other Gospels say ‘Son of God’?
questions.answer: Luke's dikaios can mean righteous, just, or innocent, reinforcing the chapter's repeated legal and moral vindication. Matthew and Mark preserve a ‘Son of God’ acclamation (Matthew 27:54; Mark 15:39). The different wording reflects each evangelist's narrative emphasis; it should be heard on Luke's own terms rather than silently replaced with the more familiar line.

questions.question: What does the torn temple veil signify?
questions.answer: Luke places the tearing just before Jesus's death amid cosmic darkness. Readers have heard judgment on the temple, opened access to God, divine grief, and the exposure of the sanctuary; Luke does not explicitly choose only one. Because the Gospel ends with disciples blessing God in the temple, the sign should not become contempt for Judaism or for Jewish worship.

questions.question: Why emphasize Joseph and the Galilean women at the burial?
questions.answer: Joseph is a council member who did not consent, preventing the leadership from becoming a faceless unanimous group. The women see exactly where and how the body is laid, prepare spices, and keep Sabbath. Their continuity from Galilee through burial to the empty tomb grounds the next chapter's testimony in named, observant witnesses.

glossary.def: Roman governor of Judea (3:1) who sentences Jesus to crucifixion despite repeated innocence declarations.
Roman public execution by suspension, designed to torture, shame, and deter.
Garden imagery used for blessed life in God's presence.
Greek adjective meaning righteous, just, or innocent; Luke's centurion applies it to Jesus.
